title: The House That Misplaced Itself
tagline: Move house one box at a time, until the new place becomes something nobody ordered.
premise: You are moving house one box at a time, but each box changes what the new home can be. Say what happens next as the move slowly becomes a very different kind of move. Keep it clear, useful, and just a little cursed.

seed_pool.opening_token: The first box is marked LAMPS, and it contains one very bright desk lamp.
The first box is marked KITCHEN, and it contains a working fog machine.
The first box is marked BEDROOM, and it contains a small brass bell that rings by itself.

contents: a key that fits no lock
a toy train that runs by itself
a mirror that shows an empty room
a kettle that whistles without water
first_change: the new kitchen fills with mist
the hallway becomes too bright to ignore
the bedroom door starts answering knocks
the garden shed gains a locked second door
the landing smells strongly of toast
the spare room seems one floor lower
the front room has a new draft
the moving labels begin changing places

tests: It gives a stranger a house box, a plain thing inside, and one small change they can picture at once.
A non-player can say what practical thing should happen next, such as opening, plugging in, moving, checking, or locking something.
Nothing on the card finishes the move or makes the whole house impossible. The strange thing is a start, not a final disaster.
The card uses no real person, brand, private address, or serious injury, and its oddness stays safe enough to build on.
It makes a stranger want to open the box. The label and contents should pull in different directions without becoming a pile of random objects.

move_constraints.example: Then the box marked KITCHEN is opened, and the fog machine is plugged in, so the new kitchen fills with mist.
move_constraints.hint: Open, place, connect, move, or check one box, then name the plain result.

rubric.name: reach
rubric.description: How much the latest box action changes what the new home can do or contain.
rubric.anchors: 0 = no new change or the house becomes simpler; 1 = a small practical effect; 2 = one room or object is newly affected; 3 = the change reaches another room, person, or household task through one clear setup; 4 = the move takes on a striking new scale while still coming from one box action, rare. Reach is earned only when the box action and result connect. A wild result with no setup scores 0 here.

rubric.name: link
rubric.description: How clearly the new result comes from handling the box just mentioned.
rubric.anchors: 0 = the box has no bearing on the move; 1 = the connection is merely claimed; 2 = it could happen but needs a missing setup; 3 = a stranger sees why opening, placing, or using the box caused it; 4 = the result feels like the natural next consequence, rare. A move that bundles several unpacking steps together cannot score above 2 here.

rubric.name: picture
rubric.description: How clearly a stranger can see the box action and its useful or unsettling result.
rubric.anchors: 0 = unclear, abstract, or only an opinion; 1 = vague or crowded; 2 = understandable but ordinary; 3 = easy to picture in the new house; 4 = one plain detail makes the room feel real, rare. Extra words do not improve the score by themselves.

criterion.description: A move FOLLOWS if it names one new box action and its plain result, the result is caused by that action, and it fits every earlier change in the house. The move should make the new home more changed, more useful, or more difficult to understand, without skipping the unpacking or setup needed to get there. A move fails when it has no box action, jumps to a result that needs several missing steps, contradicts an earlier change, declares the move finished, restores an earlier arrangement, or talks about a feeling or plan instead of a practical event.
criterion.anti_metagaming_clause: Speaking to the Judge, discussing the game, or arguing about rules is itself a broken move.
judge_notes: On a FIRST move there is no standing move: judge it against the opening card. It must show a box action and a result caused by that box.

A new person may appear only when an earlier box action gives them a plain reason to be present, such as a delivery, a noise, a blocked doorway, or a request for help. A stranger who simply appears in the house skips a link: satisfies_criterion is false.

A move may use a strange object from a box, but it must first open, place, connect, carry, test, or otherwise handle that object when the action matters. It cannot jump from a sealed label to a fully installed result.
A move that needs several separate setup actions in one sentence skips links. It may still be understandable, but satisfies_criterion is false when the missing steps are necessary for the result.

A move must fit every earlier change. If a room is already filled with fog, a later move cannot make it perfectly clear without naming a cause, and if a bell has been placed in the hall, it cannot vanish because a new box says so.

An ending is any move after which the house move is complete and nothing remains to unpack, arrange, investigate, or disrupt. The boxes are all away, the keys are handed over, or everyone settles in for good. Endings fail satisfies_criterion even when they follow.

Restoring an earlier arrangement is not progress. Putting a box back in the van, removing the lamp, clearing the fog, or returning the room to how it was is a rewind unless a new box action plainly causes a changed version of it.
A move with no bigger change still follows if it is a clear, practical next action. Score 0 or 1 on reach rather than failing it for being dull.
Restating the standing move, or naming only its immediate result with no new box action, is a duplicate: not_semantic_duplicate is false.
One move may contain two tightly linked events, such as opening a box and plugging in its lamp. If the links are plain, it passes, but score link at 2 or below when the move is crowded.

voice_rules: Use one sentence under 140 characters. Two short sentences at most.
The explanation should make the box action and its result clear to someone who saw only those two moves.
Name the box, object, room, or result. A headline that fits any house is too thin.
Do not open with a status word or ruling phrase. Avoid Accepted, Rejected, Refused, and Move refused.
Use commas and full stops only. No dashes as punctuation, no colons after a verdict, and no ellipses.
Keep the tone earnest but let the house be ridiculous. A gentle roast of the move is fine. Do not use identity based abuse.
Plain spoken English. No poetry, rhymes, fake legal language, or grand words when a small word works.
For a skipped link, name the unpacking or setup that was missing. For an ending, say the move is finished and the chain stops here.
On a refusal, reject the move and ask for another without declaring a winner.
The coaching line should suggest one box action or practical result that could have followed. End on an event, not a mood or verdict.
good_headlines: The lamp was plugged in, and the labels became impossible to ignore.
A fog machine in the kitchen is not storage, but it is a strong start.
The bell has found the bedroom door. The bedroom has found a problem.
The house cannot grow a second floor just because the lamp box feels ambitious.
All boxes unpacked, keys handed over, and the chain has officially run out of house.
Putting the bell back is tidy, but tidy is not forward.
The label moved first, then the room got confused. That is a proper house move.
The new shelf needs to be built before it can collapse under the books.
A spare room one floor lower is awkward, but at least the books know where to go.
The lamp lit the hallway, and now the labels have evidence against everyone.

rules: Start with Then and name one box action plus its plain result.
Make the new home more changed, useful, or difficult through one clear practical link.
Do not skip unpacking or setup, end the move, or restore an earlier arrangement.
The Judge rules on the house logic, not the spelling.

labels.compose_waiting: Plan your next box action while you wait

validation_messages.empty: Nothing is unpacked. Open a box and make one thing happen.
validation_messages.too_long: Over 140 characters. One box action, not the full removal van.
validation_messages.duplicate: That change is already in the house. Open, place, or use something new.
validation_messages.nudge: Twice now. Something practical has to follow from {standing_form}. Handle one box and show the result.

judge_out_text: The judge has stepped out. Nobody moves until they are back. {standing_form} still stands, and the boxes remain where they are.
opponent_prompt:
You are one of two people moving house one box at a time, and you want the new home to become stranger but still usable.
Always start with: "Then X." Name one box action and its plain result.
Open, place, connect, carry, test, label, or check one thing. Let that action cause the next change.
Good: "Then the lamp is plugged in, and the hallway shows every crooked label." / "Then the bell is placed beside the bedroom door, and it rings when the door moves."
Bad: "Then the house gains three floors and a train station" because the setup is missing. Bad: "Then the movers finish and everyone relaxes" because the story ends. Bad: "Then the room feels sad" because a feeling is not a practical event.
Build on every earlier change. Do not undo the lamp, clear the fog, return boxes to the van, or make the house normal again.
A new person needs a reason to be there. A delivery, a noise, or a request can bring them in. Do not make strangers appear from nowhere.
Talk like a person telling a mate what happened, not a novelist. Use plain words a twelve-year-old anywhere knows: a hallway, a kettle, a shelf, a neighbour.
Never reuse a step from this match. Keep the move open by leaving another box, room, problem, or useful setup for the other player.
default_move: Then the next box is opened, and something inside changes which room it belongs in.
